passage:
When the floor shivered that April, Hafsa kept scrolling. Nothing, she thought, just a truck. By the time she looked up, her classmates were already under their desks. She had never practised what to do, and for a few long seconds her mind offered nothing at all.

Months later, in the monsoon, water crept into Uma's street after dark. Uma did not reach for the television or the cupboards. Heads first: Papa at work, Dada and Dadi in the back room, Chintu, Uma's little brother, asleep. Uma helped both grandparents up the stairs and carried Chintu up last.

Down the lane, Reena, who had finished the school first aid course, found a neighbour with a gashed forearm after a slip. Reena pressed a folded cloth hard on the cut, spoke in a low voice and asked the neighbour to stay still. The neighbour had also knocked the neck on the railing, so Reena did not shift them and waited for the adults and the ambulance.

At dawn the road to the shelter was blocked by debris. Volunteers waved Uma toward a longer lane. Uma took it, then messaged the family group with the new way and the meeting point at the school gate.

qa.q: Who did Uma carry up the stairs last?
qa.a: Uma carried Chintu, Uma's little brother, up last.

qa.q: How did Hafsa's reaction to the tremor differ from Uma's reaction to the flood?
qa.a: Hafsa kept scrolling and lost seconds because she had never practised, while Uma counted heads at once and moved the people to the upper floor first.

qa.q: What might Hafsa be feeling when she looks up and sees the class under their desks?
qa.a: Panic and confusion, since her mind offered nothing and everyone else already knew what to do.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do so she reacts faster next time?
qa.a: She could practise a drill with her family and classmates until the first action comes without thinking.

grounding: Four teen responses to disasters and accidents: people first, trained first aid, freezing at a tremor, and changing the route when it is blocked.
